metadata.title: Exploring Critical Predictors of Math and Science Achievement for High Achieving Students in TIMSS Data: Application of Elastic-Net Logistic Regression

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study used TIMSS 2019 eighth-grade data for the United States and merged files via IEA IDB Analyzer (Version 5.0), then conducted modeling in R using glmnet. The manuscript does not report applying TIMSS complex survey weights (e.g., student sampling weights) or any replicate-weight variance estimation (e.g., BRR/jackknife), and no weight variable name is provided. Because the analysis is an elastic-net logistic regression with train/test splitting and 10-fold cross-validation, the authors do not describe any weight-aware estimation procedure; thus the modeling appears effectively unweighted. The main preprocessing steps reported are exclusion of cases with missing benchmark scores, dropping predictors with >10% missingness, and listwise deletion of remaining missing predictor values.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used TIMSS 2019 eighth-grade data for the United States. Dependent variables were constructed from TIMSS plausible-value-based benchmark categories (Levels 1–5) for mathematics and science; students were coded as high/advanced (1) if at least 3 of 5 benchmark values were at Levels 4–5, otherwise non-high/advanced (0). Excluded cases with missing benchmark scores. Removed predictor variables with more than 10% missing data (four variables excluded). Applied listwise deletion to remove cases with missing values across the remaining predictor variables. For model evaluation, split the resulting dataset into training (80%) and test (20%) sets, with all hyperparameter tuning (10-fold cross-validation) performed only on the training set to avoid data leakage.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Best reported model: Model 8 (AUC-based selection with λmin) — Accuracy: 77.91%, Sensitivity: 68.23%, Specificity: 83.64% (also reported: Model 6 Accuracy 77.91%, Sensitivity 68.23%, Specificity 83.64%).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Mathematics (USA) the study leveraged Home educational resources, Student confidence in science/math, Disorderly behavior during math lessons, and Sex of students to predict Mathematics proficiency level (high/advanced vs non-high/advanced), finding that Home educational resources and Student confidence were strong positive predictors while higher disruptive behavior (disorderly behavior) was associated with lower mathematics outcomes. This indicates that gifted/advanced-track selection in mathematics may benefit from interventions that strengthen students’ confidence and reduce classroom disruption, while also accounting for home-resource differences that students cannot control.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Best reported model: Model 1 (misclassification with λ1SE) — Accuracy: 70.84%, Sensitivity: 62.22%, Specificity: 77.62% (also reported: Model 5 had highest sensitivity 61.33% with Accuracy 70.83% and Specificity 78.32%).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Science (USA) the study leveraged Home educational resources, Student confidence in science/math, Sense of school belonging, and Sex of students to predict Science proficiency level (high/advanced vs non-high/advanced), finding that Home educational resources and Student confidence were consistently positive predictors while several instructional/value factors were excluded by penalization. This indicates that science advanced-level identification may be improved by supporting students’ confidence and addressing inequities in home educational resources, rather than relying primarily on instructional clarity or students’ stated value of science.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzed TIMSS 2019 eighth-grade data for the United States and created binary outcomes for mathematics and science proficiency by converting PV-based benchmark levels (Levels 1–5) into a high/advanced indicator using a majority-vote rule across five plausible-value benchmark scores. Using elastic-net logistic regression with α = 0.5 and tuning of λ via 10-fold cross-validation on the training set only, the authors evaluated models on a held-out test set using accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity. For mathematics, the best reported performance reached 77.91% accuracy with sensitivity 68.23% and specificity 83.64%; for science, the best reported performance reached 70.84% accuracy with sensitivity 62.22% and specificity 77.62%. Across both subjects, home educational resources and student confidence were the most consistently positive predictors, while some instructional/value variables were excluded by penalization. Limitations include cross-sectional TIMSS data (no causal inference), listwise deletion after dropping predictors with >10% missingness, and no reported use of TIMSS complex survey weights.
